extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of mathematics, philosophers of science, and mathematicians interested in explanation and proof methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and comparing mathematical proofs/systematizations in terms of explanatory/unifying power, stringency, embedding/subset relations of their bases, practical feasibility, and conformity to the Aristotelian ideal of purity (conservation of topic and essence-based explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unifying / explanatory power (Kitcher’s account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unifying power of a systematization is the principal measure of explanatoriness in Kitcher’s model: how well a set of argument patterns (a basis) systematizes (unifies) the target set K by generating conclusions from relatively few patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher operationalizes unifying power via quantitative comparisons (size of conclusion set and size/paucity of the basis). A systematization that generates many beliefs from a small number of patterns ranks as more explanatory. Caveats: pure quantitative comparisons can miss qualitative differences in methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of conclusion set
rubrics_metrics.description: The number (or extent) of conclusions C(·) that a systematization derives; larger conclusion sets contribute to greater unifying power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Kitcher’s ranking: if two systematizations have different conclusion sets, the one with the larger conclusion set is more unifying. If conclusion sets coincide, other criteria (e.g., basis inclusion/embedding) are used to rank them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paucity / size of the basis (number of argument patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of distinct argument patterns (the basis) required to generate the conclusion set; fewer patterns (greater paucity) count in favour of a systematization’s unifying power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher ranks a systematization with a smaller basis (or whose basis is a proper subset of another’s) as more explanatory. Beware: an infinite basis complicates comparisons; identification of 'pattern' must not be so broad as to erase meaningful distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subset relation between bases (basis inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the basis B' of one systematization is a proper subset of the basis B of another while both generate the same conclusions, then the subset systematization is more explanatory (ranks higher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit Kitcher corollary used to compare infinite bases: B' ⊂ B with C(·) equal implies the smaller-basis systematization is not equal to the best systematization E(K) of the larger. The argument depends on precise specification of bases and their instantiation sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding / translation of bases (generalized inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When no subset relation holds, one may attempt to 'embed' B' into a proper subset S⊂B via translations/correspondences between argument patterns so that conclusion sets are preserved; such an embedding would license ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal adequacy condition: an embedding must preserve conclusion sets (C). Other preservation constraints may be required but can be left informal; if B' can be embedded into a proper subset of B preserving conclusions, then B' yields a superior systematization. In practice, specifying translations/embeddings precisely can be difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of conclusion sets under embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary adequacy condition for any proposed embedding/translation between bases is that the translations of patterns from one basis produce the same conclusion set as the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding proposals that fail to preserve conclusion sets are inadequate for ranking. Preservation of conclusions is the minimal constraint; without it an embedding is not a proper basis-to-basis correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringency of argument patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Stringency is the degree to which a general argument pattern imposes demanding constraints on its instantiations — determined by (i) the required logical structure (classification) and (ii) constraints on nonlogical vocabulary in filling instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More stringent patterns (harder-to-satisfy filling/classification conditions) increase unifying power. Kitcher’s notion is underdeveloped formally, but stringency is intended to guard against trivial/uninformative generalizations. Implementation requires balancing stringency against size-of-basis and size-of-conclusion-set criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of spurious unifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematization is spurious if its filling instructions can be generalized to allow substitution of 'any sentence' (or similarly unconstrained substitutions) thereby trivializing the pattern and allowing derivation of any sentence; such patterns should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher’s explicit requirement: if filling instructions can be replaced to yield a pattern P' that derives arbitrary sentences, then P is spurious. Rationale: the remaining nonlogical vocabulary is 'idling' and imposes no real constraints. Examples: 'from α infer α' or theological-style patterns where 'α' = any accepted physical-sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of filling instructions (syntactic constraints) and classification (inferential constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a rigorous separation between filling instructions (purely syntactic constraints on substitutions for dummy letters) and classiﬁcation (which specifies inferential/logical relations among schematic sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation prevents trivialization by modifying filling instructions; classiﬁcation may impose semantic/epistemic constraints that are not captured by mere syntactic filling instructions. Properly stated classiﬁcation can block the pattern from being spurious even if filling instructions are syntactically general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly broad identification of 'argument pattern' with any derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat the notion of 'argument pattern' so broadly that it collapses into 'any derivation from axioms' — such broadness eliminates meaningful distinctions between patterns and undermines systematization comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patterns are identified with arbitrary derivations, Kitcher’s and related systematizations become vacuous (e.g., infinite patterns unavoidable); keep pattern notion restrictive enough to allow discrimination among systematizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity / applicability across domains (uniform argument patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument pattern counts as more unifying/explanatory if it applies uniformly across a relevant class of structures (e.g., uniformly to all real closed fields) rather than being specific to a single instance (e.g., just R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brumfiel values proof methods that apply uniformly to all real closed fields as exhibiting a kind of unification; Kitcher’s model should be able to reflect such uniformity as a qualitative explanatory virtue (but, in practice, may fail to do so under purely quantitative measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical feasibility / usability of argument patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond formal unifying power, an explanatory argument should be practically usable/feasible for working mathematicians (e.g., decision algorithms that are theoretically unifying but computationally infeasible may not function as paradigm explanations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tarski–Seidenberg decision algorithm can in principle unify by a single pattern but limited feasibility (complexity, impracticality) makes its arguments rarely used and thus not paradigmatic explanations in practice. Feasibility influences whether mathematicians regard a pattern as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of qualitative differences in proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative differences between methods (e.g., algebraic vs transcendental/transference methods) are relevant to explanatory assessment and may not be captured by purely quantitative measures like counts of patterns and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher’s quantitative-only approach can miss qualitative features that mathematicians treat as salient (e.g., repudiation of transcendental methods); a fuller theory should incorporate fine-grained analyses of method types and their explanatory roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of topic / purity (Aristotelian metabasis ex allo genos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity: do not 'cross from one genus to another' in a proof; demonstrations should conserve the subject-matter/topic (the 'what') and rely on knowledge appropriate to that domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle saw purity as an ideal of highest proofs — e.g., 'We cannot ... prove geometrical truths by arithmetic.' Preservation of topic supports extension of genuine 'what'-knowledge and prevents misleading cross-domain reductions that obscure the cause/essence of the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence-based explanation (showing the cause in the subject’s 'whatness')
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality (pure) proof should show that the predicate of the theorem holds of the subject because of the subject’s essence (definition, 'whatness'); proofs that ground explanation in essential features provide superior epistemic understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: demonstrative knowledge requires knowledge of the cause (aitia) tied to the essence; in mathematics the 'why' should ultimately trace to definitions (e.g., definition of straight line). Such essence-based explanations are epistemically privileged over proofs that rely on external or cross-domain principles.
